This was in the second year of the Changqing era. It is currently visible on stone tablets at Zhongli in Haozhou. The record of the Sixth Patriarch’s interpretation is provided hereafter. Therefore—
There is no explanation. It is preserved here as well.
○ Chapter Twenty-Two: No Dharma Can Be Attained.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, when the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was it for...”
"Is it that there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti.
In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained; this is what is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Subhūti said, "The exhaustion of the mind that seeks attainment is itself bodhi. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
Regarding bodhi, I truly have no mind of seeking, nor do I have a mind of attainment.
Because of this, it is named 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi' (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment)."
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Section on Purifying the Mind and Practicing Goodness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By means of non-self, non-person, non-being, and non-living entity, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
Then one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This Dharma of enlightenment—from the Buddhas above down to the smallest insects—entirely contains the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) and is no different from that of a Buddha;
therefore, it is called "equality," being without high or low. Because enlightenment is non-dual, one merely abandons the four [extremes].

Regarding the marks: if one cultivates all wholesome dharmas while not being free from the four marks, then even as one cultivates all wholesome dharmas, the mind that seeks to realize liberation through the notions of self and person will only increase further; there would be no way to attain it. If, however, one is free from the four marks...
By practicing all wholesome dharmas, liberation may be expected. To practice all wholesome dharmas means to have no defiled attachment toward any dharma;
to remain unmoved and unshaken in the face of any object; to be without craving, clinging, or affection for supramundane dharmas;
and to constantly employ skillful means in all places, acting in accordance with sentient beings to bring them joy.
With joyful faith, they submit. For them, he preaches the True Dharma, causing them to awaken to Bodhi. Only in this way can it be called "cultivation.

Therefore, it is said: "One must cultivate all wholesome dharmas. Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely named "wholesome dharmas."
To cultivate all wholesome dharmas while hoping for their karmic rewards is not, in itself, a wholesome dharma.
To ardently perform the six perfections and the myriad practices without the mind seeking recompense is what is called a wholesome dharma.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Incomparable Merit of Wisdom and Virtue.

Subhūti, if there were someone who took as much of the seven treasures as all the Sumeru kings in the three-thousandfold world system and used them to practice giving, yet another person were to take this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*—
Even if one were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from it, the former merit would not equal a hundredth part of this;
it would not equal a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
Mount Mahācakravāḍa is two million two hundred twenty-four thousand li in height and breadth;
Mount Cakravāḍa is one million one hundred twelve thousand li in height and breadth; and Mount Sumeru is three million three hundred sixty thousand li in height and breadth.

This is what is called a "trichiliocosm" (three-thousandfold great thousand-world system). Speaking in terms of principle, this refers to the fact that each of greed, hatred, delusion, and false conceptualization possesses one thousand [aspects].

Even if mountains as numerous as these were all like Mount Sumeru, and one were to take them as an analogy for the quantity of the seven treasures used in giving, the merit obtained would be immeasurable and boundless; yet it remains ultimately a cause of outflow (*āsrava*). And...

There is no principle of liberation [attained through other means]. Although the four-line sūtra of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is brief, by practicing in accordance with it, one immediately attains Buddhahood.
Thus, we know that the merit of upholding this sūtra can cause sentient beings to realize bodhi;
therefore, it cannot be compared [to other merits].
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Transformation of Those Not to be Transformed.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti’s thought was that the Tathāgata possessed a mind that delivers sentient beings;
the Buddha, in order to dispel such a doubt in Subhūti’s mind, said: "Do not conceive such a thought. All sentient beings are fundamentally and inherently Buddhas. If one says...
If the Tathāgata were to save sentient beings and cause them to become Buddhas, that would be a false speech.
Because it would be a false speech, it would entail the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. This is intended to dispel the mind that clings to "self.

Now, although all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, if they do not rely on the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma, there is no way for them to awaken by themselves; depending on what could they practice to achieve [enlightenment]?
"Buddha-way.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a 'self,' it is not that there is a self; yet ordinary people think there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called 'ordinary people' by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary people; they are merely designated as 'ordinary people.'"
When the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," he refers to the self that is intrinsically pure—the self of permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity.
This is not the same as the self of ordinary beings, which is characterized by greed, hatred, ignorance, delusion, and unreality. Therefore, it is said that ordinary beings conceive of a self;
those who possess such a conception of a person are indeed ordinary beings. When the conception of a self and a person does not arise, one is no longer an ordinary being.
If the mind undergoes arising and ceasing, one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). If the mind is without arising and ceasing, one is not an ordinary person.
If one does not awaken to the *prajñāpāramitā*, one is an ordinary person. If one awakens to the *prajñāpāramitā*, one is not an ordinary person.
If the mind possesses subject and object, one is an ordinary person. If the mind is without subject and object, one is not an ordinary person.
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied, “So it is, so it is;
the Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, “Subhūti, if one were to... [continue as in the source text]”
Regarding those who view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks: a wheel-turning sage king would then be the Tathāgata. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, perceived that Subhūti’s affliction of clinging to marks had not yet been eliminated; thus, he posed this question.
Subhūti, not yet understanding the Buddha’s intention, replied, "So it is, so it is. Such words already constitute a deluded mind;
to further say that one should view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks is another layer of delusion, moving ever further away from the truth.

Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke for them to eliminate that deluded mind. If one were to perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) would be the Tathāgata.
Although a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the thirty-two marks, how could he be the same as the Tathāgata?
The World-Honored One cited these words in order to dispel Subhūti’s ailment of clinging to marks.
This caused his realization to penetrate deeply to its source. When Subhūti was questioned, his deluded mind was instantly resolved;
thus he said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
Subhūti was a great Arhat who had attained profound realization and possessed skillful means; he did not fall into error, but sought instead to clarify the World-Honored One’s intent.
He eliminates subtle delusions so that sentient beings of future generations shall not err in their perception.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me through sound, Such a person follows a deviant path And cannot see the Tathāgata."
If one considers these two characters, they serve as the opening of the discourse. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to appearance; "seeing" (*darśana*) refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Self" (*ātman*) refers to the essence of intrinsic purity within the bodies of all sentient beings—the unconditioned, signless, true, and eternal substance.
One cannot achieve accomplishment by reciting the Buddha’s name with a loud voice; rather, one must maintain right mindfulness with clarity to attain awakening and understanding.

If one seeks [the Buddha] through forms and sounds, He cannot be seen. Thus we know that to contemplate the Buddha within appearances and seek the Dharma within sounds is for the mind to be subject to arising and ceasing, and such a person will not awaken to the Tathāgata.
Chapter Twenty-seven: On Neither Annihilation nor Extinction Subhūti, if you should think:
"The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of perfection," Subhūti, do not think thus. The Tathāgata has not [attained it] by means of the marks of perfection.

Therefore, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, if you should think that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speak of the characteristic of the annihilation and cessation of all phenomena, do not think so.
Why is this? Those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of [the annihilation] of phenomena.
The characteristic of annihilation.
Having heard it said that the true body is free from characteristics, Subhūti then thought that one could attain bodhi without cultivating the thirty-two marks of purification.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Do not say that the Tathāgata did not cultivate the thirty-two marks of purification."

And thus one attains bodhi. If you were to say that one attains unexcelled bodhi without cultivating the thirty-two pure practices, that would be to sever the lineage of the Buddhas; such a thing is impossible.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: On Non-Attachment and Non-Greed.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River and offer them as a gift;
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is another person who understands that all phenomena are without self and attains patience, this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept meritorious blessings.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
“Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with craving; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”
To penetrate all phenomena without the mind of subject or object is called "patience" (kṣānti).
The merit obtained by such a person surpasses the merit of the aforementioned seven treasures. The merit produced by a bodhisattva is not for their own sake;
since their intention lies in benefiting all sentient beings, it is said that they do not "receive" merit.

Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Tranquility of Dignified Conduct Subhūti, if anyone should say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
He is named the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata neither comes nor does not come; neither goes nor does not go; neither sits nor does not sit;
neither lies down nor does not lie down. Amidst the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying—he is always in emptiness and stillness; this is precisely the Tathāgata.
He comes. ○ Chapter Thirty: The Principle of the Unified Whole.
Subhūti, if a good man or a good woman were to take this great trichiliocosm and grind it into fine dust,
"Particles. What do you think? Is this multitude of minute particles great or not? "Very great, World-Honored One. "For what reason?
If this multitude of minute particles were substantially existent, the Buddha would not have called it a 'multitude of minute particles. Why is that?"
The Buddha spoke of a multitude of atoms; yet that which is called a multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms—it is merely designated as such.
The Buddha spoke of a trichiliocosm to serve as a metaphor for the number of atoms upon the nature of all sentient beings.
Just as there are all the atoms within a trichiliocosm, so too are there [atoms] upon the nature of all sentient beings.
Delusive thoughts are like motes of dust; yet these motes of dust are not truly motes of dust. Upon hearing this sutra and awakening to the Way, one’s enlightened wisdom shines constantly.
As one proceeds toward Bodhi, every thought-moment does not abide, remaining perpetually pure. Such pure motes of dust are what are called the "multitude of motes of dust."
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata refers to as the "trichiliocosm" is not a world; it is merely designated as a "world.
To speak in terms of principle, the "three thousand" signifies that greed, anger, ignorance, and deluded thoughts each possess one thousand aspects.
The mind is the pivot of good and evil; it can create both the ordinary and the sagely. Its movement and stillness cannot be measured;
vast and boundless, it is therefore called the Great Trichiliocosm.
Why is this? If a world were a truly existent entity, it would be a "single integrated mass. Yet what the Tathāgata calls a "single integrated mass" is not a single integrated mass;
it is merely designated as a "single integrated mass."
Within the mind, nothing surpasses the two dharmas of compassion and wisdom. It is by means of these two dharmas that one attains bodhi.

To speak of a "unified mark" (ekaghanākāra) is because the mind still dwells upon what is attained; therefore, it is not a unified mark. When the mind has no attainment, this is called the unified mark.
As for the unified mark, one cannot grasp it through provisional names, but must discourse upon the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Subhūti, that which is a "unified mark" is ultimately ineffable; yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.
Through the two dharmas of compassion and wisdom, one accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi, which cannot be fully described and is wondrous beyond words.
Ordinary people are greedily attached to words and activities; they do not practice the two dharmas of compassion and wisdom.
If one does not practice these two dharmas of compassion and wisdom while seeking unsurpassed bodhi, by what means could it ever be attained?
Chapter Thirty-one: On the Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision.
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span," Subhūti, what do you think?
Would that person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One. That person would not."

One understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this? When the World-Honored One speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span;
they are merely designated as "the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span."
When the Tathāgata speaks this sutra, he causes all sentient beings to personally awaken to the wisdom of *prajñā* and to personally cultivate the fruit of *bodhi*.
Ordinary people, failing to understand the Buddha’s intention, claim that the Tathāgata speaks of views such as a self (*ātman*) or a person (*pudgala*);
they do not know that the Tathāgata speaks of the profound, signless, and unconditioned *prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding the Dharma: the views of self, person, and so forth spoken of by the Tathāgata are not the same as the views of self, person, and so forth held by ordinary beings.
When the Tathāgata says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is the "view of the True Self.

When he says that all sentient beings possess untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) which is inherently complete by nature, this is the "view of the Person" (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). When he says that all sentient beings are fundamentally without [defilement],...
“Afflictions” is the view of a sentient being. To say that all sentient beings are by nature fundamentally neither born nor extinguished is the view of a life-principle (*jīva*).
Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, [regard them as follows...]
Knowing thus, seeing thus, and resolving with faith thus, one does not give rise to the mark of dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called the "mark of dharmas" has been taught by the Tathāgata as being no mark of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "mark of dharmas."
One who has resolved to attain Bodhicitta should perceive that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;

they should perceive that all sentient beings are inherently endowed with the untainted seeds of wisdom. They should have faith that the self-nature of all sentient beings is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
Although they employ all forms of wisdom and skillful means to engage with others and benefit living beings, they do not conceive of subject and object.
If one speaks of the dharma of signlessness with the mouth while the mind still possesses subject and object, this is not the characteristic of the Dharma.

If one speaks of the dharma of signlessness with the mouth and practices the conduct of signlessness with the mind such that the mind of subject and object is extinguished, this is called the characteristic of the Dharma.
Chapter Thirty-Two: On the Non-Reality of Manifestations.
Subhūti, if there were someone who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, were to offer them as a gift;
and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and holds this sutra—even for a moment...
To receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain even as little as four lines of verse for others brings merit far superior to that. How does one explain it for others?
Without grasping at signs, remaining unmoving in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*).
Although the merit of the seven treasures may be vast, it does not equal that of a person who gives rise to the bodhicitta, upholds even four lines of this sutra, and expounds them for others;
the latter’s merit surpasses the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, beyond all analogy.

To skillfully employ expedient means in preaching the Dharma, observing the faculties of others and responding according to their measure, in various ways as is appropriate—this is what is meant by "expounding for others."
Those who listen to the Dharma possess various and unequal physical appearances; one must not give rise to a discriminating mind.

Rather, one should realize the mind that is empty, quiescent, and suchness (tathatā)—a mind that has nothing to be attained, a mind free from competition, a mind free from expectation, and a mind free from arising and ceasing. This is called "suchness-immovability."
Why is this? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way:
that which is a dream is the false body; that which is an illusion is false thought; that which is a bubble is affliction (*kleśa*); and that which is a shadow is karma.

Obstructions, dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows—these are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Reality is free from names and signs; for the awakened one, there are no such karmic activities.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās...]
Upāsikā. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all those in the world—devas, humans, and asuras—were filled with great joy;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

Postscript to the Oral Instructions of the Sixth Patriarch:

The Dharma-nature is perfectly quiescent; fundamentally, it is without arising or ceasing. Because the thought of arising occurs, there subsequently arises the conditions for birth; thus, Tiande received his mandate.
This is what gives rise to life; therefore, it is called destiny (*ming*). Once the mandate of Heaven is established, the ultimate emptiness enters into existence.

The thoughts of the previous day transform into the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The function of this mental consciousness disperses to become the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Each of these six faculties possesses its own discrimination.
That which is the totality within is therefore called the mind (*citta*). The mind is the locus of thought and deliberation;
it is the abode of the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is where the true and the false coexist. It is the ground where ordinary beings and sages nearly meet.
That all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been unable to transcend birth and death is entirely due to this.
The mind is that which is burdened by afflictions; therefore, the Buddhas teach only that people must understand this mind. Once this mind is understood, one sees one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
To see one's own nature is itself *bodhi*. When this [nature] exists as its own essence, it is entirely empty and quiescent, serene and as if non-existent.
Conditioned by birth, there arises thought; thereafter, there is existence. Where there is birth, there is form. Form is a congealed froth of earth, water, fire, and wind.
It takes blood and breath as its substance and serves as the locus for that which has come into being. When blood and breath are sufficient, the essence (*bindu*) is sufficient;
when the essence is sufficient, spirit (*śen*) is produced. When spirit is sufficient, wondrous function (*myōyū*) is produced. Thus, this wondrous function is precisely...
This is my true self at the time of my parinirvāṇa. Because the physical form encounters objects, it is manifested merely through action.
However, ordinary people are deluded and pursue objects, while sages and worthies are enlightened and respond to objects. Those who pursue objects do so from their own [delusion].
To respond to phenomena is to follow the self; to follow them from the perspective of "the other" is to become attached to what is seen, and thus one seeks through saṃsāra.

That which is the self is, in its very substance, eternally empty; throughout ten thousand kalpas, it remains as it is. When viewed in their totality, these are all the wondrous functions of the mind.
Therefore, at the time when they have not yet arisen, that which is called "nature" is perfectly complete and replete; it is void and without thing, profoundly still and self-abiding.
However, my vastness is equal to empty space; I come and go and manifest transformations with complete freedom.
Although the gods might wish to command me to take birth, how could they succeed? If even the gods cannot command me to take birth, how much less so the four great elements?

How much more so regarding the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*)! Since there are both the thought of arising and the conditions for arising, Heaven is able to give me life, the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are able to form my body through their vital energy, and the five elements are able to instruct and constrain me.

This is why that which has birth must have cessation. Thus, birth and cessation are one and the same; they are what distinguish the ordinary person from the sage in their process of arising and ceasing.

Thus they differ. Ordinary people give rise to thoughts conditioned by existence; consciousness transforms according to karma, and as it is permeated by habitual tendencies, birth increases all the more.

Therefore, once born, the mind clings to various delusions: it falsely identifies the four elements as its own body, falsely identifies its six kin as its own possessions, falsely identifies forms and sounds as happiness, and falsely identifies worldly toil as...
For the sake of wealth and status, the mind perceives and knows nothing that is not false. Once these delusions arise, the afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest in ten thousand variations.
Delusive thoughts usurp the truth, and the true nature (*tathatā*) consequently becomes obscured. With the notions of self and other acting as the host, the true consciousness becomes a guest.

The three karmas (*trikarma*) lead the way in front, followed by a hundred subsequent karmic actions. One drifts through birth and death without end; when birth is exhausted, there is extinction, and when extinction is exhausted, one is born again. Thus it continues in birth...

The characteristic of cessation follows in succession until one falls into the various realms of existence. Abiding within these realms, one wanders on and on without awareness, further indulging in ignorance and weaving the nets of karma.

Thus, even when the kalpas as numerous as dust motes and sands have ended, one no longer attains a human body. The noble sages, however, are not like this. The birth of the noble sages does not depend on [karmic] thought;
they appear through the manifestation of traces. When they wish to be born, they are born, without waiting for that [karmic] destiny. Therefore, once they are born...
Afterwards, the nature of perfect quiescence remains as before, profoundly still; it is without substance or form and free from all obstruction.

Its illumination of the myriad dharmas is like the bright sun in a clear blue sky, without the slightest bit of concealment or stagnation. Thus, it establishes all wholesome dharmas, pervading the entirety of the dust-motes of the universe.
One does not perceive even a slight [self] as it gathers in all sentient beings and returns them to quiescence;

yet one does not regard this as much. Driven, it cannot come; pursued, it cannot go. Although it relies upon the four great elements to form a body and the five phases to provide nourishment, these are all merely what I have borrowed;
I have never falsely identified with them. When the conditions for the "I" are exhausted, the traces of the "I" shall naturally perish; I shall abandon them and depart, just as the Tathāgata did.
It departs; what concern is it to me? Therefore, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born, they undergo extinction; that which is extinguished cannot but cease to be.
When noble sages (*ārya*) are born, they likewise undergo extinction; yet that which is extinguished returns to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Thus, the birth and extinction of ordinary beings are like shadows within the body—they follow one another in coming and going without end. The birth and extinction of noble sages are like [clouds] in the sky.

Thunder arises and ceases of its own accord; it does not burden other things. People of the world do not realize that arising and ceasing are like this, and thus they regard arising and ceasing as a great affliction and calamity.
This is because they lack self-awareness. If one were aware, one would see arising and ceasing as dust upon the body—something to be shaken off with a single vigorous movement.
How could they then give rise to attachment toward my nature? In the past, our Tathāgata, out of great compassion...
The mind takes pity on all sentient beings who are thus deluded, inverted, and wandering through the cycle of birth and death.

Furthermore, seeing that all sentient beings possess the inherently existing nature of bliss and sovereignty, and that they are all capable of practicing and realizing Buddhahood, [the Bodhisattva] desires that all sentient beings may entirely undergo the arising and ceasing of sages and worthies, rather than the arising and ceasing of ordinary worldlings. Yet, [the Bodhisattva] still fears that all sentient beings lack...
Since the beginning, we have wandered for a long time; our dispositions have already diverged, and it is impossible for all to attain sudden enlightenment through a single teaching.
Therefore, eighty-four thousand dharma-gates have been expounded. Each gate provides entry, and each leads to the ground of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
In expounding each dharma-gate, every word is earnest and truthful, intended to enable all sentient beings to follow their own perceptions.
This Dharma gate involves entering one's own mind-ground, reaching one's own mind-ground, seeing one's own Buddha-nature, and realizing one's own Buddha-body;

thus, one is identical to the Tathāgata. Therefore, when the Tathāgata speaks of "existence" in various sutras, it is because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to give rise to wholesome roots by beholding signs.

When he speaks of "non-existence," it is because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to leave behind signs and see their nature. His teachings on the emptiness of form are likewise [for this purpose].
It is likewise so. Yet sentient beings cling to their perceptions; they see existence, yet it is not true existence, and they see non-existence, yet it is not true non-existence.

Their seeing of form and their seeing of emptiness are both instances of such clinging. Furthermore, they give rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, which become the very root of birth and death.
Since the Dharma-gate of non-duality is not shown to them, they continue to wander through birth and death in confusion, delusion, and inversion even more intensely than before.

The day before yesterday, the Tathāgata once again expounded the Great Prajñā Dharma for us, shattering the two views of permanence and annihilation, so that all sentient beings may know that true existence and true non-existence, true form and true emptiness, are fundamentally non-dual. Furthermore, they are not distant from people;
they are profoundly still and tranquil, existing solely within one's own nature. One need only use the wisdom of one's own nature to illuminate and shatter all delusions.

Thus, one clearly perceives for oneself. For this reason, throughout the six hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Tathāgata expounds the Buddha-nature for those bodhisattvas who have attained the fruit;
yet, within it, there are still portions taught for those of the sudden and gradual vehicles.

Only the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is taught for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle. Therefore, that sūtra first explains the four [dharmas].
The four marks of arising are produced. Next, it says: "Whatever has marks is all empty and false. If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
This reveals that when all phenomena reach the state of non-abiding, this constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Therefore, in this sutra, whenever the Tathāgata speaks of anything pertaining to existence, he immediately refutes it; for he seeks the true reality beyond the provisional in order to demonstrate it to sentient beings. Indeed...
It is because they fear that sentient beings will fail to understand what is taught, as their minds would instead become fixated on something.

This is as in the case of the saying, "The Buddha-dharma is itself not the Buddha-dharma," and so forth. Therefore, when the Great Master Huineng was receiving the robe and the transmission of the Dharma from the Fifth Patriarch, upon hearing this sutra recited—specifically the words, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere"—he attained great enlightenment at that very moment.
This is the sixth patriarch. The Tathāgata said that all Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas, all emerge from this sutra.
Is it not true? I recently read the *Dān jīng* (The Sutra on Almsgiving) and heard that the Sixth Patriarch attained the realization of his nature through this sutra;
I suspected there must be some exposition [of it], yet I had not seen it. Then I learned of Cao...
I am from Jiyin Prefecture. At the residence of Mr. Xing Jingu, I obtained a copy of the Sixth Patriarch’s Oral Instructions (*kǒujié*).
Observing that its language is concise and direct, its judgments clear and decisive, it enables people to understand easily without confusion. My joy was beyond measure.

Furthermore, I reflect that the people of Jingdong, Hebei, and Shaanxi are by nature simple, honest, and sincere; when faced with matters, they act with resolute decisiveness. If they were made to study the Buddha-nature...
They are certainly able to be courageous and diligent, surpassing others; yet those who serve as lecturers mostly transmit only the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* and the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above*.
Their students do not understand that the myriad phenomena arise according to conditions, and that when conditions are exhausted, phenomena must likewise cease.

Instead, they treat phenomena as if they were inherently real, stubbornly clinging to them and consequently becoming bound by these very phenomena. Thus, at death, they do not know how to liberate themselves.
It is like a person sinking in sand who struggles against it with all their might; the more they exert force, the deeper they sink.
They do not realize that by ceasing to struggle against the sand, they could emerge from the mire. This is truly a great pity.

I have therefore intended to carve the oral instructions for the Sixth Patriarch’s *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* onto woodblocks to circulate them, so as to awaken the Buddha-nature of these several students. However, because the text was extensive, many portions were omitted.
[This was] an error. Consequently, I sought out other editions over a period of ten years and obtained eight in total. Only those from Hangzhou, Yue, Jian, and Shan were largely identical;

thus, I was able to correct the errors and establish the definitive text. Master Dong Zun earnestly encouraged me to complete this work, and he further exhorted the officials of the court to provide the funds for hiring craftsmen.
Upon hearing of this, all the literati were delighted to offer their assistance. [Among them was] Master Lou of Siming.
I have always aspired to seek out this matter to its conclusion. Alas! The Tathāgata said, "That which cannot be spoken of is called the teaching of the Dharma.
Indeed, that which can be perceived through words and letters—how could that be the true reality of the Buddha-dharma?
Yet, were it not for words and letters, the true reality could not be transmitted. Therefore, students must rely upon the oral instructions of the Sixth Patriarch to seek the gold.
The Diamond Sutra: By means of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one seeks one's own Buddha-nature;

having seen one's own Buddha-nature, one then realizes that the Buddha-dharma does not consist merely of oral instructions. If this is so, how could the merit of the Sixth Patriarch regarding the Buddha-dharma be conceivable?
Some, because the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate, suspect that these oral instructions were not composed by him. This is, for example—
Now, how could the Great Canon have been composed by the World-Honored One himself? It was also transmitted by those who heard the Dharma.
Whether it was spoken by the Sixth Patriarch and then passed down by his disciples, I cannot know for certain.
If the scriptures can be understood through oral instructions, why should one doubt that he was illiterate?

regarding the various scriptures of the Buddha’s teachings, I have never previously investigated them extensively. Furthermore, as my circumstances have been such that...

Amidst the many hardships and the mundane affairs of the dusty world, it is truly said that one is but "flesh for the eyes. Recently, I heard that Great Master Shitang has traveled with his staff to Haihui Temple on Mount Wu.

His compassionate clouds spread and his Dharma rain falls, reaching as far as Jing; those who look toward him in admiration and pay their respects are countless, and they have consequently given rise to the great Bodhicitta.
Ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, he first proclaimed the supreme and wondrous meaning of the *Vajra*.
I, too, had the opportunity to listen attentively from among the great assembly for ten days;

upon inquiring about the Master’s interpretation of the *Vajracchedikā*, I found it truly to be "opening the ears of the deaf and clearing the eyes of the blind," its brilliance penetrating with perfect clarity. Regarding the commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā* produced since ancient times, which one do you consider the most excellent?
The Master replied, "There are no fewer than a thousand schools of interpretation, yet those whom I have long respected and trusted are only these: [he then recited the titles].
The Sixth Patriarch’s commentary is the foremost; yet, although it has circulated for a long time, its printing blocks have remained submerged.
Previously, I made a vow to reprint it, but alas, my strength was insufficient and circumstances were difficult, so I have not had the leisure to undertake the task. Alas!
How vast and inexhaustible was the Master’s compassionate grace in saving the world! Though I am not clever, I request to set the woodblocks in motion, thereby completing the Master’s work.
Zhi: Although it was the Master’s wish, I requested it; why then do you say it is my carving? Zu explained it, and the Master transmitted it;

why then do you say it is the Master’s carving? It is simply to ensure that for all eternity, throughout the world and future generations, this interpretation shall circulate widely, so that everyone may know it exists, and all may be able to abide in non-characteristic and non-abiding, thereby subduing their minds. This is the Master’s wish.
This may perhaps offer some slight consolation.

In the fifth month of the summer of the *guisi* year of the Shunzhi era, the disciple from Qiantang, Tang Yisheng, washed his hands and prostrated himself to compose this postscript for the re-engraving of the Sixth Patriarch’s Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra.

By nature, I am simple and unadorned, and do not indulge in frivolous luxury. Whenever I hear the sound of the great bell or the chanting of the *brahmans*, my countenance is invariably moved with joy.

I have lingered here for ten days, unable to bear the thought of departing; this is not solely due to the inspiration awakened by the scriptures, but is also the result of my innate disposition cultivated from former lives.
Last year, I stayed with the Lord of Wei-yang at the provincial office in Rongzhou; it was somewhat removed from the dust and clamor of the secular world.

On the night of the Yuanxiao festival, while viewing lanterns on the broad streets, he heard the sound of Chan recitation. He went to the master’s quarters and obtained a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with commentaries by the Sixth Patriarch.
Its principles were extensively expounded and its phrasing was transcendent; upon reading it once, he understood it clearly, as if illuminated by a thousand suns rising at once.
Having been hindered by a lack of karmic affinity, he now realized what the Sixth Patriarch had meant when he said, "I heard [the Dharma] in a guest house."

Those who attain realization through the sutras and those who do so through [the patriarchal teachings] are of one and the same essence. How magnificent! Our Buddha’s wondrous realization is profound and deep;
it sweeps away all attachments, causing every person to disperse the clouds of doubt and clearly penetrate the celestial realm of their own nature.

The Patriarchs explored the obscure and elucidated the abstruse, penetrating directly to the true source. Truly, there is not a single dharma that does not serve as a bridge; even the five aggregates are entirely utilized for this purpose.
This is a scripture for those seeking liberation. There are no fewer than several hundred commentaries on this sutra, yet only that of the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, is the most supreme.
Having obtained it, I rejoice and receive it upon my head;

it is indeed that which all Buddhas have protected with their mindfulness and entrusted to us. How could I dare not engrave it upon my bones and carve it into my flesh, so as to together repay the radiance of their grace?

Therefore, I have contributed funds for the carving of woodblocks so that it may be widely circulated. This shall enable those who read the sutra to understand its essential meaning and, through such understanding, attain its source.
It will brilliantly illuminate the school of the nature (Xingzong), extinguishing all empty phenomena. Thus, one neither dwells upon appearances nor destroys appearances.
How could the merit of this act of giving possibly be compared to those who seek [the Dharma] through forms or sounds? Respectfully inscribed.
